## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet, and scores stay hidden for the whole search. That means later rounds will only tell us whether trials crashed or failed the checks, not how well they did. So each candidate should be a well-reasoned bet that could beat the baseline. The budget is fixed at about 131k samples, roughly 32 PPO updates with the default recipe. A network smaller than the baseline doesn't buy extra samples (r is floored at 1), so the network should stay close to r≈1. The likely gains are better use of samples (more policy updates) and better per-footprint perception. A placement builds the target exactly only if the brick's landing layer, which is the highest point under its footprint, matches target cells that are still missing at that layer, without sealing target cells underneath. Each column's own stack carries that information, so per-column stem features should reach the footprint-pooling head directly. Plan: one change to the recipe only, one change to the network only, and one candidate that combines both.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials trained without errors at about the starting compute (r≈1.04–1.08). Scores are hidden, so nothing has been measured as better or worse yet, and with 2 seeds a few points could be noise anyway. So I am choosing ideas from the structure of the task. A placement is correct when the layer the brick lands on (the highest build cell under the footprint) has target cells missing across the whole footprint, and when the brick does not cover missing target cells lower down. The network has to work this out per layer and pool it over the footprint. The column-skip head (r1c2) is a reasonable base because it gives the head per-column features without the blurring of the 3x3 convs. This round tries three different ideas: (1) a richer footprint head that also sees the raw observation through its learned projection, (2) global self-attention for context across the board, and (3) a new per-layer footprint head. That head pools over each footprint separately for each layer, and learned cumulative sums tell it what is below and above each layer.

### Round 3
All six trials trained without errors, but scores are hidden, so no lineage can be ranked. Every sample already costs at least as much as the baseline's, so extra network cost only removes samples, and cheap changes are the safer bet. Not yet tested: (1) receptive field. The baseline's two 3x3 convs see only a 5x5 window on the 8x8 grid, but placement order depends on distant supports and overhangs. (2) Recipe settings other than batch size: discount and GAE lambda (credit for the +1 exact-build bonus at episode end), and the epoch count, which trades gradient steps for more samples. Each proposal makes one main change to the cheap column-skip network (r1c2), so whichever one the real scores pick is a clean result.

### Round 4
Scores are hidden, so these choices come from reasoning, not measured results. All earlier trials trained without errors. The column-skip head is the most plausible network gain because it costs almost nothing (r≈1.08). The costlier options (attention, per-layer head, wider head) leave fewer training samples. Exact-build success depends on the +1 bonus at episode end, which gamma 0.95 heavily discounts, so gamma 0.99 with lambda 0.95 is the recipe change most likely to help. Fewer PPO epochs (2) give about 1.8x more fresh designs, which should help generalisation. In this last round I combine these plausible gains: (A) column-skip with long horizon and the sample-heavy recipe; (B) dilated full-grid context with long horizon; (C) a new idea, the legality mask reshaped to per-type maps and fed in as learned input, which hints at landing height near the top of the stack, with long horizon.

## Trial it ended with
name: Column-skip + dilated context conv
hypothesis: Adds a third residual 3x3 conv with dilation 2 to r1c2. The receptive field grows from 5x5 to about 9x9, which covers the whole 8x8 grid. The agent can then see distant missing cells and the supports an overhang needs, which governs the safe build order, and DONE and value get better features. Cost is about r=1.35. Refuted if it scores no better than r1c2. That would mean decisions are local and the samples it costs are wasted.
